title: Ordinary divided-power polynomial extension
statement: Let $C$ be a commutative ring and $I\subset C$ an ideal with an ordinary divided-power structure $\gamma$ [def-sfb-ordinary-divided-power-structure]. For an integer $t\geq1$ form the free $C$-module $P=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^t}C X^{[\alpha]}$ with unit $X^{[0]}$ and multiplication $X^{[\alpha]}X^{[\beta]}=\prod_{j=1}^t\binom{\alpha_j+\beta_j}{\alpha_j}X^{[\alpha+\beta]}$. This is a commutative unital $C$-algebra. Put $P_+=\bigoplus_{\alpha\neq0}C X^{[\alpha]}$ and $K=IP+P_+$. There is a unique ordinary divided-power structure $\delta$ on $K$ restricting to $\gamma$ on $I$ and satisfying $\delta_n(X_j)=X_j^{[n]}$ for $n\geq1$. For any commutative ring $D$ with an ordinary divided-power ideal $(L,\eta)$, any unital ring map $f:C\to D$ with $f(I)\subset L$ and $f(\gamma_n(x))=\eta_n(f(x))$, and any $z_1,\ldots,z_t\in L$, there is a unique unital ring map $F:P\to D$ extending $f$, preserving divided powers on $K$, and sending $X_j$ to $z_j$; it sends $X^{[\alpha]}$ to $\prod_j\eta_{\alpha_j}(z_j)$. Here an ordinary divided-power structure $\eta$ on an ideal $L$ of a commutative ring $D$ means maps $\eta_n:L\to L$ for $n\geq1$, with $\eta_0(z)=1$, satisfying $\eta_1(z)=z$, $\eta_n(dz)=d^n\eta_n(z)$, $\eta_n(z+w)=\sum_{i=0}^n\eta_i(z)\eta_{n-i}(w)$, $\eta_n(z)\eta_m(z)=\binom{n+m}{n}\eta_{n+m}(z)$ and $\eta_n(\eta_m(z))=\frac{(nm)!}{n!(m!)^n}\eta_{nm}(z)$ for $d\in D$, $z,w\in L$, and $n,m\geq1$. The factorial quotients are integer coefficients, not divisions in $D$.

proof.text: Write $e_\alpha=X^{[\alpha]}$ and $b(\alpha,\beta)=\prod_j\binom{\alpha_j+\beta_j}{\alpha_j}$. Extend the displayed multiplication $C$-bilinearly. Its associativity follows from the integer identity $b(\alpha,\beta)b(\alpha+\beta,\lambda)=b(\beta,\lambda)b(\alpha,\beta+\lambda)$: in coordinate $j$ both sides are the multinomial coefficient $(\alpha_j+\beta_j+\lambda_j)!/(\alpha_j!\beta_j!\lambda_j!)$. Symmetry gives commutativity and $b(0,\alpha)=1$ gives the unit. Constants form a unital copy of $C$, and the positive-degree span is an ideal because a sum of nonnegative multi-indices with one nonzero is nonzero. This proves the claimed algebra and augmentation descriptions.

proof.text: For $\alpha\ne0$ and $n\geq1$ set $c(n,\alpha)=\prod_j(n\alpha_j)!/(n!\prod_j(\alpha_j!)^n)$. This is an integer: take, for each $j$, a labelled set of size $n\alpha_j$ and an ordered decomposition into $n$ blocks of size $\alpha_j$. Simultaneous permutation of the block labels acts freely on the tuples of decompositions, because at least one $\alpha_j>0$. Each orbit has $n!$ elements, giving precisely this quotient. Multiplying basis elements repeatedly gives $e_\alpha^n=n!c(n,\alpha)e_{n\alpha}$. Over any ring $R$ whose additive group is torsion-free, the free module $P_R$ is also torsion-free, coefficient by coefficient. Apply the factorial-divisibility criterion to its ideal $(P_R)_+$, generated by the $e_\alpha$ with $\alpha\ne0$. It supplies a divided-power structure $\theta$ with $\theta_n(e_\alpha)=c(n,\alpha)e_{n\alpha}$. In particular $\theta_n(X_j)=e_{n\mathbf e_j}$ since $c(n,\mathbf e_j)=1$.

source.place: Tag 07H5 (lemma-divided-power-polynomial-algebra), torsion-free augmentation construction using Tag 07GM (lemma-silly)(4); same multi-variable argument

proof.text: Take $R=\mathbf Z[T_c:c\in C]$ and the evaluation $q:R\to C$ sending $T_c$ to $c$, using the polynomial-ring definition and evaluation formula. It is surjective because each $c$ is the image of $T_c$, and $R$ is torsion-free by its unique finite monomial expansion over $\mathbf Z$. Let $\mathfrak a=\ker q$. The coefficientwise surjective ring map $P_R\to P_C$ has kernel $\bigoplus_\alpha\mathfrak a e_\alpha$ and maps $(P_R)_+$ onto $(P_C)_+$. If $u=\sum_{\alpha\ne0}a_\alpha e_\alpha$ belongs to the kernel, all $a_\alpha\in\mathfrak a$. The addition and scalar axioms expand $\theta_n(u)$ as the finite sum, over $\sum_\alpha k_\alpha=n$, of $\prod_\alpha a_\alpha^{k_\alpha}\theta_{k_\alpha}(e_\alpha)$. For $n>0$ each term has a factor in $\mathfrak a$ and positive degree. Thus the kernel intersection is stable. Apply surjective descent to obtain $\theta$ on $P_+$; its formula on $e_\alpha$ is still $c(n,\alpha)e_{n\alpha}$. No factorial is inverted in $C$.

proof.text: The displayed basis makes $P$ a free $C$-module, hence flat by the cited free-module clause. Flat extension therefore gives a divided-power structure $\bar\gamma$ on $IP$ extending $\gamma$. Coefficientwise, $IP$ consists of finite expansions with every coefficient in $I$, while $P_+$ has zero constant coefficient. Hence $IP\cap P_+=\bigoplus_{\alpha\ne0}I e_\alpha=IP\cdot P_+$: each $a e_\alpha$ on the middle expression is the product of the constant $a\in I$ and $e_\alpha\in P_+$, and the reverse containment follows since both are ideals. The product-agreement assertion says $\bar\gamma$ and $\theta$ agree on this intersection. Apply the gluing assertion to obtain $\delta$ on $K=IP+P_+$ restricting to both. It extends $\gamma$ and satisfies $\delta_n(X_j)=X_j^{[n]}$ by step 3.

To prove uniqueness let $\delta\prime$ be any structure with the required values. For $\alpha
e0$ choose $j$ with $m=\alpha_j>0$ and put $v=\prod_{k
e j}X_k^{[\alpha_k]}$, so $e_\alpha=v\delta\prime_m(X_j)$. The scalar and composition axioms give $\delta\prime_n(e_\alpha)=v^n rac{(nm)!}{n!(m!)^n}X_j^{[nm]}=c(n,\alpha)e_{n\alpha}$; here $v^n=\prod_{k
e j} rac{(n\alpha_k)!}{(\alpha_k!)^n}X_k^{[n\alpha_k]}$ by repeated basis multiplication. These are equalities with integer coefficients. Thus $\delta\prime$ and $\delta$ agree on every positive basis element and on $I$. These elements generate $K$ as an ideal. Equality extends to scalar multiples by the scalar axiom and then to finite sums by repeated use of the addition axiom, proving uniqueness.

proof.text: For the specified $f$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_t$, define on finite expansions $F(\sum a_\alpha e_\alpha)=\sum f(a_\alpha)\prod_j\eta_{\alpha_j}(z_j)$. It is additive, unital and extends $f$. For basis products the divided-power multiplication axiom in $D$ gives $\prod_j\eta_{\alpha_j}(z_j)\prod_j\eta_{\beta_j}(z_j)=b(\alpha,\beta)\prod_j\eta_{\alpha_j+\beta_j}(z_j)$; distributing finite sums now proves multiplicativity. It sends $X_j$ to $z_j$. Moreover $F(K)\subseteq L$: constants from $I$ map to $L$ by hypothesis, and the image of each positive monomial contains a factor $\eta_r(z_j)\in L$ with $r>0$.

proof.text: For $\alpha\ne0$ select $j$ and $m=\alpha_j>0$ as in step 5. Apply the scalar and composition axioms to $\prod_k\eta_{\alpha_k}(z_k)$ in $L$. Repeatedly using $\eta_r(z)\eta_s(z)=\binom{r+s}{r}\eta_{r+s}(z)$ for the other factors gives $\eta_n(F(e_\alpha))=c(n,\alpha)\prod_k\eta_{n\alpha_k}(z_k)=F(\delta_n(e_\alpha))$. On constants from $I$ preservation is the hypothesis on $f$. For a scalar multiple $pg$ of either kind of generator, preservation follows from $F(p^n\delta_n(g))=F(p)^n\eta_n(F(g))$. For a finite sum of these, expand both sides using the addition axiom; the sums agree term by term. Thus $F$ preserves divided powers on all of $K$. Finally any such ring map must send $X_j^{[r]}=\delta_r(X_j)$ to $\eta_r(z_j)$, and hence every $e_\alpha=\prod_jX_j^{[\alpha_j]}$ to the stated product. Additivity and extension of $f$ force the displayed formula for every element, proving uniqueness.
